d: The Halifax area's history museum, in a historic bank building on Beach Street. Start here for the story of Daytona, Ormond, Holly Hill and the Halifax River towns. (Jeep Michelle volunteers with the Halifax Historical Society.)
First lit in 1887 and 175 feet tall, it is the tallest lighthouse in Florida. Climb to the top for a view of the inlet and both coasts of the peninsula.

n: Mary McLeod Bethune Home & Bethune-Cookman University
a: 640 Dr Mary McLeod Bethune Blvd, Daytona Beach
d: In 1904 Mary McLeod Bethune opened a school here with $1.50 and five girls. It grew into Bethune-Cookman University, and her campus home is a National Historic Landmark.
On March 17, 1946, the City Island ballpark let Jackie Robinson take the field for his first integrated spring training game, a year before he broke Major League Baseball's color barrier.
NASCAR was born here. Bill France Sr. began the organizing meetings in the rooftop Ebony Club on December 14, 1947.

a: 1801 W International Speedway Blvd, Daytona Beach
d: Opened in 1959, the year Lee Petty won the first Daytona 500. Before the Speedway, stock cars raced on a combined beach-and-road course.

a: Granada Blvd at A1A, Ormond Beach
d: Honors the early automobile speed trials that ran on the hard-packed Ormond-Daytona beach starting in 1903, which earned Ormond Beach its nickname.
John D. Rockefeller's winter home on the Halifax River, now a city cultural center with exhibits and riverside gardens.
Site of the Timucuan village of Nocoroco, where the Tomoka and Halifax rivers meet. Great for paddling and oak-shaded picnics.

a: 950 Old Sugar Mill Rd, Port Orange
d: Coquina and iron remains of a sugar mill destroyed during the Second Seminole War, surrounded by botanical gardens. Look for the concrete dinosaurs left from the 1940s Bongoland attraction.

a: Old Mission Rd, New Smyrna Beach
d: Coquina walls of an 1830s sugar mill burned during the Second Seminole War. A short, shady walk and one of the best-preserved ruins in the county.

a: Riverside Dr & Julia St, New Smyrna Beach
d: A large coquina foundation on a bluff over the Indian River. It is often tied to Andrew Turnbull's 1768 colony, though historians still debate who built it.
Tells the story of the 1768 New Smyrna colony, when more than 1,400 settlers, mostly from Minorca, arrived to work Andrew Turnbull's plantation.

a: A1A, south of New Smyrna Beach
d: A towering Timucuan shell mound built from oyster shells over centuries, one of the largest on Florida's Atlantic coast. A boardwalk leads to the top.

a: 601 Ponce de Leon Blvd, De Leon Springs
d: A spring with a long history of Timucuan use and later plantations. At the Old Spanish Sugar Mill restaurant you cook your own pancakes right at the table.
Winter home for hundreds of manatees, plus the 1872 Thursby House, built by an early settler family on top of a shell mound.
Hat maker John B. Stetson's 1886 winter estate, often called Florida's first luxury winter home. Tours are by reservation.
Founded in 1883 as DeLand Academy and later renamed for its benefactor, John B. Stetson. The historic campus sits at the north end of downtown DeLand, the county seat since 1887.
A spiritualist community founded in 1894, with a historic district of Victorian-era cottages and a hotel from the 1920s.
A historic 1880s church in Enterprise, the town that served as Volusia County's first county seat before DeLand took over in 1887.
Just over the county line: coquina sugar mill ruins from a plantation burned in 1836 during the Second Seminole War. Worth the drive up Old Kings Road.
